content: More than 25% of the reviewed literature exaggerated conclusions by attributing outcomes and impacts to interventions without proper study designs or by relying on unverified data sources or anecdotal evidence. Among the 14 quantitative evaluations included in the review, a statistically significant increase in private or shared latrine construction was observed in intervention groups compared to control groups. The declaration or certification of open defecation-free (ODF) status was the second most common indicator, but no consistent definition of ODF was reported. However, there was limited evidence to determine whether sustained sanitation behavior change or health impacts resulted from CLTS interventions. A qualitative content analysis of the literature identified several factors influencing the implementation and effectiveness of CLTS. Among 21 implementation-related factors, the most frequently cited were government awareness and buy-in for CLTS, local government ownership, institutional capacity, and the quality of triggering activities. Regarding community-related factors, the most commonly reported were community participation, access to financial and technical resources, climate conditions, and expectations of latrine subsidies. Despite these findings, systematic research on the CLTS implementation process and its adaptations was minimal. An exploratory review by Williams and Overbo (2015) examined the effectiveness of sanitation interventions in reducing environmental fecal contamination. The review highlighted that many sanitation systems, such as pit latrines, septic tanks, and sewerage systems, fail to prevent the unsafe return of human excreta to the environment. Issues such as unlined pits, damaged facilities, and improper sludge disposal were common. In some cases, pit latrines were vulnerable to storms, rainfall, and flooding. Septic tanks and latrine pits were often not emptied, and untreated liquid waste was discharged into open drains or groundwater sources. A review by Sclar et al. Of the 29 eligible studies, 23 examined transmission pathways, and six assessed drinking water contamination based on proximity to sanitation facilities. The outcomes included microbiological assessments of drinking water, hand contamination, soil contamination, and the presence of flies or feces. The results showed mixed effects, with most studies reporting no significant impact on transmission pathways. However, some evidence suggested sanitation interventions were associated with reduced fly populations and observed feces, though these findings were not statistically significant. Freeman et al. (2017) updated systematic reviews on the health impacts of sanitation interventions, including infectious diseases and nutritional outcomes. The review included 171 eligible studies, with 84 used in meta-analyses. Greater access to sanitation was associated with significantly lower odds of diarrhea (12% reduction overall, 23% reduction in intervention studies) and lower odds of soil-transmitted helminth (STH) infections, ranging from 20% to 52% reductions. Improved sanitation access was also protective against schistosomiasis and active trachoma and positively associated with height-for-age. However, the evidence quality was rated low to very low, and most studies used observational designs. Speich et al. (2016) reviewed the effects of sanitation on intestinal protozoa infections, finding significant reductions in infections like Entamoeba histolytica and Giardia intestinalis with improved sanitation. Majorin et al. (2018) reviewed interventions for safe disposal of child feces, finding lower odds of diarrhea when child feces were disposed of in toilets. However, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) showed limited evidence of impact on helminth infections. Ejmot-Nwadiaro et al. (2015) reviewed handwashing promotion, concluding it likely reduces diarrhea episodes by about 30% in both high-income and lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). However, long-term maintenance of handwashing habits remains poorly understood. Yates et al. (2015) reviewed the impact of water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) interventions on people living with HIV, finding that lack of household sanitation was a significant risk factor for intestinal parasites and diarrhea morbidity. Sclar et al. (2017) reviewed the effects of sanitation on cognitive development and school absence, finding some evidence of improved cognitive ability but inconsistent findings on school absence. The quality of evidence for both outcomes was rated very low. Sclar et al. (2018) examined the relationship between sanitation and personal well-being, identifying eight aspects of well-being (e.g., privacy, safety, dignity) influenced by sanitation. The review highlighted the experiences of women and girls but noted limited generalizability due to the focus on specific populations. A systematic review by Overbo et al. (2016) examined the role of policy and enabling environment factors in sanitation adoption and sustained use. Political will, leadership, and coordination between sectors were critical for program success. Access to credit and community mobilization also supported adoption. Cultural norms, physical barriers (e.g., flooding), and implementation activities (e.g., house visits, mass media) influenced outcomes. Monitoring and evaluation were essential for strategic planning and accountability. However, many contextual factors were interdependent, requiring effective planning and lesson-learning to address barriers.
